doc.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

read_this_first: The interview was recorded eleven years after Liston's 1985 stroke. She had memory loss and difficulty speaking; her turns are short and the transcriber replaced stretches with bracketed summaries. No pull_quote here contains a transcriber's summary. `stands_alone: false` means the line needs the exchange around it -- it is in `exchange`. Bryant's dates and facts are Bryant's: check `liston_response`, Liston often corrects or cannot confirm them. Timeline entries with stated_by 'bryant' or 'transcriber' and confirmed_by_liston false are not her testimony.

categories.label: Beginnings
categories.definition: Her childhood and youth before she turned professional: family, Kansas City, the move to Los Angeles, school, the first trombone, and Alma Hightower's youth band.

categories.label: The Big Bands
categories.definition: Her working life as a member of other leaders' bands, from the Lincoln Theater pit band through Gerald Wilson, Count Basie and Dizzy Gillespie, including touring with them and the State Department tours.

categories.label: Being a Woman
categories.definition: Lines whose point is that she was a woman in a man's music: how audiences, bandmates, the business and other women treated her, and what women musicians face.

categories.label: Playing and Singing
categories.definition: Her own playing and performing as an adult: the instrument, her sound and solos, what she thinks about when she blows, singing her own numbers, and her struggle to play again after the stroke.

categories.label: Arranging
categories.definition: Her writing: how she began, how she works, writing from the soul, writing for leaders, singers and strings, her compositions, and how she and others react to hearing her arrangements.

categories.label: Life Offstage
categories.definition: The parts of her life apart from making music: the years she left music for day jobs, her film roles, her marriages and loves, and home.

categories.label: Randy Weston
categories.definition: Her forty-year partnership with the pianist Randy Weston: how they met, the albums she arranged for him, how they work together, and his standing by her.

categories.label: Teaching the Young
categories.definition: Her work with young musicians and what she thinks of them: the youth orchestras, the Jamaica years, her advice to students, and her view of young players and music today.

categories.label: Bandleader and Business
categories.definition: Her career under her own name and the business around it: her own groups and records, managers, labels, money, credit and recognition.

categories.label: The Stroke and After
categories.definition: The 1985 stroke and the years to the interview: losing speech and thought, recovery, fear of being seen, friends who helped, writing again, life in Los Angeles, plans to return to New York, and taking stock of her life.

items.event: Born in Kansas City, Missouri; grandparents lived in Kansas City, Kansas, and she grew up between the two.
items.notes: Date from the transcript header; birthplace in her own words.

items.event: Went to school in Kansas City, Kansas, staying with her grandfather during the week and her mother at weekends.
items.notes: Partly a transcriber summary inside Bryant's turn; Liston does not respond directly.

items.event: Grew up with a player piano at home (the same piano she still owned in 1996); attended Unity church.
Had a radio show in Kansas as a child performer ('I was a little star').
Saw a trombone and asked her mother to buy it that same day.
items.notes: Age from a transcriber summary of Bryant's question; Liston confirms the story by mentioning a tape of her mother describing it. Year derived from age 7.

items.when: about five months after getting the horn
items.event: Was playing Deep River and Rocking the Cradle of the Deep, learned from the radio; turned her head sideways to reach the far slide positions.
items.notes: Year derived.

items.event: Took two or three lessons from a Kansas City teacher she disliked, then had her mother cancel him.
Moved to California (Los Angeles); grandmother and aunts went first, she and her mother followed four or five months later by train.
Enrolled at McKinley Junior High School; tested for ninth grade but was placed in eighth because of her age.
Her school music teacher wanted to adopt her to send her to special schools; she refused to leave her mother.
Met Minnie Hightower at school and joined Alma Hightower's youth band; practised at the Ross Snyder playground; played alongside Vi Redd and Alice Young.
Travelled with Miss Hightower and the Melodic Dots in the back of a truck to play a fair—her first time on the road.
items.notes: Year proposed by Bryant; Liston answers 'Uh-huh'.

items.event: Photographed with the Hightower band (Minnie Hightower, Vi Redd, Buddy Redd and others).
items.notes: Liston: 'It was '38 or something like that.'

items.event: Attended Jefferson High School briefly and mainly Polytechnic High School, with Minnie Hightower.
items.notes: From a transcriber's bracketed summary.

items.event: Herb Jeffries played the Lincoln; the Lincoln and the white downtown theatres were separate worlds.
items.notes: Liston says '19 – whatever it is – 40', which sits a little before the age-16 (1942) start at the Lincoln implied in 295571; the transcript's figures are recorded as given.

items.event: Left Hightower, joined the musicians' union and started working in the pit band at the Lincoln Theater.
items.notes: Year derived from her stated age of 16 (born 1926).

items.event: Bandleader Bardu Ali had her write music for acts that arrived without charts—the start of her writing career; also performed skits with Pigmeat Markham.
items.notes: Year derived.

items.when: after a year or a year and a half at the Lincoln
items.event: Joined Gerald Wilson's band ('he stole me out of the band'); first job with him at Shepp's Playhouse; worked as copyist and sometime arranger.
items.notes: Year derived from 'a year or a year and a half' at the Lincoln.

items.event: Spent 5–6 years (Wilson says 8) with Gerald Wilson; played Chicago and New York, including a show with Jimmie Lunceford and the Apollo, where she sang and played features.
Toured the South with the Wilson band behind Billie Holiday; the tour collapsed and the band was stranded, getting only as far as Kansas City.
Recorded with Count Basie, according to Gerald Wilson.
items.notes: Liston does not remember recording with Basie.

items.event: Recorded with Dexter Gordon, a schoolmate—her first recording and first time playing without written music.
items.notes: Year and 'first recording' stated by Bryant; Liston confirms the session.

items.event: Joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band in New York (with John Coltrane in it); Billy Eckstine told her Dizzy had held the chair empty a week; the band lasted five months and broke up.
Returned to Los Angeles and Gerald Wilson.
Took the Board of Education exam on her own and worked there two or three years (clerical, night school), taking occasional gigs.
Quit, tried playing again, then worked at the Golden State insurance company before quitting to return to music.
Dizzy Gillespie sent for her again; she went back to New York to stay.
items.notes: Year given by Bryant ('I think '49'); elsewhere Bryant refers to 'the '56 band with Dizzy' (295704). Recorded as the transcript gives it.

items.event: In Gillespie's '56 band; some band members resented a woman being sent for from the West Coast until they played her arrangement; stayed until the band broke up.
Met Randy Weston at Birdland while playing with Gillespie; arranged his album with Little Niles—the start of a 40-year partnership ('56 to '96).

State Department tours with Gillespie to the Middle East and South America (and the Far East); wrote a medley of Ellington, Basie and others for the tour; her Annie's Dance arrangement was well received.
Appeared in the films The Ten Commandments and The Prodigal (as Lana Turner's maid).
Arranged Gloria Lynne's album with strings, including her own songs Love, I've Found You and We Never Kissed; was sick on the recording date so Quincy Jones conducted.
Worked for Ray Charles for two or three years.
Recorded as leader (Melba and Her 'Bones); recording arranged by Leonard Feather.

Helped establish youth orchestras—the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra (1964), the Harlem Back Street Tour Orchestra, Pratt Institute Youth in Action—writing and directing; also spent two or three years going to Philadelphia.
Arranged Little Niles and Hi-Fly for Randy Weston's Tanjah.
items.notes: Liston does not explicitly confirm the date.

items.event: Went to Jamaica with Randy Weston and taught there five or six years; left when the island's leadership changed.
Jamaica jazz festival, with Frank Foster and Dexter Gordon; she was carrying two horns but not playing.
Invited to the Women's Jazz Festival in Kansas City.
items.notes: Liston does not remember the organisers' names; the confirmation is a transcriber summary.

items.event: Went back to Jamaica to finish the school year, spent about two weeks in St. Lucia, then returned to New York and bought an apartment.
items.notes: 'Was that still '79?' is Bryant's question; Liston does not answer it directly.

items.event: Married Nelson Harris (her second husband); her tune Len Sirrah is his name backwards; they later separated.
Started her own all-women group in New York, toured the East Coast and China, then gradually replaced women with men (Melba Liston and Company, with Budd Johnson and Al Grey).
Suffered a stroke, causing memory loss and difficulty speaking.
items.notes: Liston refers to 'the stroke' throughout but not to its year.

items.event: Named an NEA Jazz Master.
items.notes: From the transcript header only.

items.event: Major Holley took her downtown and helped her buy her first computer.
items.notes: Year from Bryant ('When we were in New York—what? – '88 or something').

items.event: Her trombone was stolen.
Moved to Los Angeles; continued writing only for Randy Weston.
Arranged Randy Weston's Earth Birth (strings; recorded in Montreal), unreleased at the time of the interview.
Her husband died while visiting his mother in South Carolina, a few months before the interview.

items.when: 1996, about a month before the interview
items.event: Susan Slaughter of the International Women's Brass Conference sent her a new trombone.
Interviewed by Clora Bryant at her home in Los Angeles for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program.
Planned to return to New York for Christmas after six or seven years in Los Angeles.
Died.
items.notes: From the transcript header only.
